name: Anti-Money Laundering Regulation
evidence_rating: thin: not yet applicable (from July 2027); no evaluation; general literature sceptical of AML effectiveness and documents unintended costs (de-risking, credit)
summary: The Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, which applies from July 2027, replaces national rules with a single EU rulebook, caps cash payments at EUR 10,000 and is backed by a new EU authority costing about EUR 40 million a year. The Commission did not estimate how much money laundering it would prevent, and nothing has yet been measured. Wider research is sceptical: one review finds anti-money-laundering rules remove less than 0.1% of criminal money, and studies document side effects such as banks dropping whole groups of customers and cutting lending to small firms.

indicators.objective: The proposal's financial statement has no LFS indicators; the memorandum promises a first review five years after application (the AMLR applies from 10 July 2027). Indicators below come from section 9 of the impact assessment

indicators.indicator: Number of suspicious transaction reports (STRs) transmitted to law enforcement
indicators.evidence: Not yet measurable (Regulation applies from July 2027). Baseline: Europol (2017) found only around 10% of STRs lead to further investigation and about 1% of criminal proceeds are confiscated.

indicators.indicator: STRs generated by the non-financial sector; proportion of STRs usable for financial intelligence
indicators.evidence: Not yet measurable; no baseline series published by the Commission.

indicators.indicator: Volume and nature of information exchanged among FIUs (FIU.net); feedback to obliged entities
indicators.evidence: Not yet measurable; AMLA (which hosts the FIU support mechanism) only began operating in 2025.

indicators.indicator: Reduction of undetected money laundering/terrorist financing (estimated by Europol at well over EUR 100bn a year); EUR 10,000 cash-payment ceiling to 'significantly deter' laundering without hurting financial inclusion
indicators.evidence: Not measured; the IA itself says undetected laundering cannot be measured. Independent work questions the effectiveness of the AML model in general (Pol 2020: less than 0.1% impact on criminal finances) and documents unintended costs such as de-risking (EBA 2022) and reduced lending to small firms (Slutzky et al., Colombia).
indicators.sources: SWD(2021) 191; Pol 2020; EBA 2022; Slutzky et al.

indicators.indicator: AMLA running cost about EUR 40m a year at 250 FTE, over half financed by levies on obliged entities; bank-register interconnection about EUR 2m; lower compliance costs for cross-border financial groups

literature.citation: European Commission (2021), Impact Assessment accompanying the Anti-money laundering package (executive summary SWD(2021) 191), SWD(2021) 190
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the Anti-money laundering package (executive summary SWD(2021) 191)
literature.method: ex-ante (qualitative; cost estimates for new Authority)
literature.outcomes: money laundering detection; compliance costs; supervision
literature.headline: More consistent rules and an EU authority expected to reduce undetected ML/TF (Europol estimate: well over EUR 100bn/yr); EUR 10,000 cash ceiling; AMLA cost about EUR 40m/yr; lower compliance costs for cross-border institutions; monitoring via STR counts, STR quality and FIU information exchange
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected harmonised rules, a cash-payment cap and a new EU authority to cut money laundering, at a cost of about EUR 40 million a year for the authority, but gave no estimate of how much laundering would fall.
literature.verified: full text read (executive summary and monitoring section)

literature.citation: Pol, R.F. (2020), Anti-money laundering: The world's least effective policy experiment? Together, we can fix it, Policy Design and Practice 3(1): 73-94
literature.title: Anti-money laundering: The world's least effective policy experiment? Together, we can fix it
literature.method: review and synthesis of published estimates (global)
literature.headline: AML policy has less than 0.1% impact on criminal finances; compliance costs exceed recovered criminal funds more than a hundred times over; data poorly validated so findings not definitive
literature.summary_plain: A widely cited review estimates that anti-money-laundering rules worldwide remove less than 0.1% of criminal money while costing over a hundred times more than they recover, though the data are weak.
literature.quality: synthesis of weak data; not specific to the AMLR

literature.citation: Slutzky, P., Villamizar-Villegas, M. & Williams, T. (2026), Drug money and bank lending: the unintended consequences of anti-money laundering policies, Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization (earlier IIEP Working Paper 2019-5)
literature.authors: Slutzky, P., Villamizar-Villegas, M. & Williams, T.
literature.title: Drug money and bank lending: the unintended consequences of anti-money laundering policies
literature.venue: Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization (earlier IIEP Working Paper 2019-5)
literature.method: difference-in-differences (Colombia's 2008 SARLAFT AML reform; bank-municipality and bank-firm credit data)
literature.outcomes: deposits; bank lending; firm sales, investment, employment
literature.headline: After the AML reform deposits fell in high drug-trafficking municipalities; banks reliant on those deposits cut lending elsewhere; small firms dependent on affected banks saw lower sales, investment, profitability and employment
literature.summary_plain: A study of a Colombian anti-money-laundering reform found it drained deposits from drug-trafficking areas, leading banks to cut lending to small firms elsewhere, which then invested and hired less.

literature.citation: European Banking Authority (2022), Opinion of the European Banking Authority on 'de-risking' (EBA/Op/2022/01), EBA, 5 January 2022
literature.title: Opinion of the European Banking Authority on 'de-risking' (EBA/Op/2022/01)
literature.method: survey of competent authorities and stakeholders (2020-21)
literature.headline: De-risking occurs across the EU and affects payment and e-money institutions, asylum seekers from high-risk jurisdictions and non-profits; can cause adverse economic outcomes or financial exclusion; scale cannot be quantified for lack of statistics
literature.summary_plain: The EU banking authority found banks across the EU drop whole groups of customers - payment firms, charities, asylum seekers - to avoid money-laundering risk, causing financial exclusion, though it could not measure how much.

literature.citation: Rice, T., von Peter, G. & Boar, C. (2020), On the global retreat of correspondent banks, BIS Quarterly Review, March 2020
literature.authors: Rice, T., von Peter, G. & Boar, C.
literature.title: On the global retreat of correspondent banks
literature.method: descriptive panel analysis of SWIFT data, 2011-2018
literature.headline: Active correspondent banks fell about 20% since 2011; jurisdictions with weaker governance and AML controls lost more relationships; payments may shift to less regulated channels
literature.summary_plain: BIS research shows the number of active correspondent banks fell about 20% since 2011, hitting countries with weaker anti-money-laundering controls hardest and potentially pushing payments into less regulated channels.

literature.citation: European Court of Auditors (2021), EU efforts to fight money laundering in the banking sector are fragmented and implementation is insufficient (Special report 13/2021), ECA Special report 13/2021
literature.title: EU efforts to fight money laundering in the banking sector are fragmented and implementation is insufficient (Special report 13/2021)
literature.headline: Institutional fragmentation and poor coordination at EU level; supervision national with insufficient EU oversight; limited EU tools to ensure application of AML rules
literature.summary_plain: The EU's auditors found pre-reform anti-money-laundering supervision fragmented and weakly enforced - the problem the AMLR and new EU authority aim to fix.

literature.citation: Europol (2017), From suspicion to action: Converting financial intelligence into greater operational impact, Europol
literature.title: From suspicion to action: Converting financial intelligence into greater operational impact
literature.headline: Only around 10% of STRs lead to further investigation; barely 1% of criminal proceeds in the EU are confiscated
literature.summary_plain: Europol found only about one in ten suspicious-transaction reports is investigated further and barely 1% of criminal proceeds are confiscated - a baseline for judging the AMLR.
